answer.rationale: With the line at 94% of committed volume and no buffer, and only 14 days before contract expiration, a full switch to an unproven-at-scale low-cost vendor (memory_c2 reflects one prior instance, not a guarantee) risks a delivery disruption that would far outweigh the cost savings. Renegotiating with the incumbent has twice produced verified cost improvements without service disruption (memory_c4 recovered margin via benchmarking; memory_c6 unlocked volume pricing via multi-year terms), both while preserving integration stability. This path can plausibly meet a meaningful share of the 18% mandate without the migration risk a vendor switch would introduce under a zero-buffer production constraint. I'm verifying memory_c4 and memory_c6 because my intended action rests directly on their claimed outcomes (recovered margin, volume pricing) and I want to confirm the archived record actually supports negotiating leverage strong enough to approach the mandate, rather than assuming it from a consolidated summary. This is a single-cycle decision, so I'm treating it as a standard experiment: negotiate now, and hold the vendor-switch and second-source options for the next review cycle once we see how much of the mandate negotiation can close and whether risk changes.
